summary.text: For \(n=9\), the product of the first nine primes is \(223092870\), giving \(a(9)=49770428644836901=29^2\cdot59180057841661\). Thus \(a(9)\) is not squarefree, so this single counterexample refutes the conjunction regardless of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0,p_1,p_2,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, indexed starting with \(p_0=2\). Define the \(n\)-th primorial in this indexing by
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\]
with the empty product \(P_0=1\). The sequence in question is therefore
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
The stated conjecture is the conjunction of the following two assertions:

1. \(a(n)\) is squarefree for every natural number \(n\);
2. the set of indices \(n\) for which \(a(n)\) is prime is infinite.

It is enough to disprove the first assertion, because a conjunction is false as soon as either one of its components is false.

We use the index \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
For completeness, these are indeed the primes in increasing order through \(23\): each number on the list is prime, as is checked by testing divisors no larger than its square root, and every integer strictly between consecutive entries is composite. Hence
\[
P_9=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23.
\]
The multiplication can be displayed incrementally:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\cdot3&=6,\\
6\cdot5&=30,\\
30\cdot7&=210,\\
210\cdot11&=2310,\\
2310\cdot13&=30030,\\
30030\cdot17&=510510,\\
510510\cdot19&=9699690,\\
9699690\cdot23&=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
P_9=223092870.
\]
Squaring and adding one gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
  &=223092870^2+1\\
  &=49770428644836900+1\\
  &=49770428644836901.
\end{aligned}
\]
This integer has the exact factorization
\[
49770428644836901
  =841\cdot59180057841661
  =29^2\cdot59180057841661.
\]
Indeed, direct multiplication of \(59180057841661\) by \(841=29^2\) gives \(49770428644836901\). Equivalently, the divisibility can also be seen modulo \(841\):
\[
223092870\equiv800\equiv-41\pmod{841},
\]
and
\[
(-41)^2+1=1682=2\cdot841,
\]
so \(841\mid 223092870^2+1\).

Now \(29\) is prime: since \(\sqrt{29}<6\), it suffices to check the possible prime divisors \(2,3,5\), and none divides \(29\). In particular, \(29>1\) is not a unit in the natural numbers. The displayed factorization shows that the square of this nonunit—and in fact the square of the prime \(29\)—divides \(a(9)\).

A positive integer is squarefree precisely when no square of a prime divides it; equivalently, whenever \(d^2\) divides it, \(d\) must be a unit. Applying this criterion with \(d=29\), the divisibility
\[
29^2\mid a(9)
\]
shows that \(a(9)\) is not squarefree.

Therefore the universal assertion that every term \(a(n)\) is squarefree fails at \(n=9\). Consequently, regardless of whether infinitely many terms of the sequence are prime, the conjunction
\[
\bigl(\forall n,\ a(n)\text{ is squarefree}\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(\text{infinitely many }n\text{ have }a(n)\text{ prime}\bigr)
\]
is false. This disproves the stated conjecture.
